```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(csvschema)
```

A CSV passed between programs is a one-way broadcast over an erasure channel:
rows vanish, cells get damaged, and there is no way to ask the sender for a
resend. The internet solved the same problem decades ago by assuming a hostile
channel and encoding everything else. `csvschema` borrows three of its ideas:
fragmentation metadata, per-piece integrity, and whole-object verification.

## A packet is one ASCII token

Every piece of the schema is a single unquoted token of the form
`{{<id>~<payload>~<crc>}}`. No comma, semicolon, tab, pipe, quote, newline, or
whitespace appears inside it, so no CSV dialect ever needs to quote it and no
delimiter rewriting can change it. Non-ASCII bytes are percent-encoded and
spaces become `+`:

```{r}
cs_encode_token("Public charity")
cs_encode_token("Café")
```

Here are the actual packets for a small schema:

```{r}
s <- cs_schema(
  data.frame(ein = "001234567", year = 2020L, rev = 1.5,
             org = factor("Public charity"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  primary_key = "ein",
  overrides = list(ein = list(constraints = list(pattern = "^[0-9]{9}$",
                                                 unique = TRUE)))
)
writeLines(cs_packetize(s, mtu = 200))
```

Packet `S0` is the header (wire version, encoding, dialect, field count, row
count, MTU, and the whole-schema hash). Packets `S1`..`Sn` are the fields in
column order, and the last schema packet carries table-level properties such as
the primary key. Each packet's attribute keys map one-to-one onto Frictionless
Table Schema v2 field properties, so the sidecar and the packets are two
encodings of the same model.

## Three internet ideas, translated

```{r echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Internet = c("IP identification", "IP fragment offset",
               "IP more-fragments flag", "TCP/UDP checksum, Ethernet CRC",
               "BitTorrent info-hash", "TCP retransmission",
               "PAR2 / fountain codes", "Path MTU"),
  Purpose = c("group fragments of one datagram", "position of this piece",
              "know when all pieces are in", "discard damaged pieces",
              "reject mixed versions", "recover loss via back-channel",
              "recover loss with no back-channel", "max piece the link accepts"),
  csvschema = c("schema hash in packet 0", "k in S<k>/<P>",
                "P carried in every packet", "CRC-32 suffix per packet",
                "whole-schema hash recomputed after reassembly",
                "not available; repetition coding instead",
                "repetition now; erasure type reserved", "mtu argument")
), col.names = c("Internet mechanism", "Purpose", "csvschema analogue"))
```

Each packet carries its own index *and* the total count, rather than a
last-piece flag, because a flag fails when the last piece is the one lost. Each
packet ends with a CRC-32 over `id~payload`; a packet that fails is dropped as
if its row had been deleted. After reassembly, the whole-schema hash in packet
0 is recomputed --- so a plausible mix of two schema versions is rejected even
though every individual packet is valid.

```{r}
rec <- cs_recover(cs_parse_packets(cs_packetize(s)))
rec$status
```

## How much redundancy?

Repetition coding makes survival a coupon-collector problem. If a fraction *f*
of rows is kept at random and each packet has *r* independent copies, a union
bound over *P* packets gives the minimum copies as
`ceiling( ln(P / eps) / -ln(1 - f) )`, which `cs_copies()` computes:

```{r}
f <- c(0.50, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05, 0.01)
data.frame(
  retained = f,
  copies   = vapply(f, function(fi) cs_copies(20, fi, eps = 1e-6), integer(1))
)
```

`cs_redundancy()` turns a required *r* into a concrete layout --- a number of
schema columns *c* and packets per cell *p* --- preferring extra packets per
cell (invisible) over extra columns, and `cs_survival()` reports the achieved
failure probability for any layout:

```{r}
cs_redundancy(20, 2000, f = 0.2)$sentence
cs_survival(20, 2000, c = 1, p = 1, f = 0.2)
```

## Striping

Random row loss is the easy case. Structured loss --- a `head()`, a page of a
paginated export, a systematic every-*k*-th sample --- is handled by a
deterministic rotating stripe, so the packets are spread rather than clustered.
`cs_stripe()` is pure arithmetic, so it is reproducible and testable:

```{r}
cs_stripe(P = 4, N = 8, c = 1, p = 1)
```

The stripe guarantees that the first `P` rows contain every packet (so a
`head()` recovers), that any `2P - 1` consecutive rows do, that a full read
does, and that the systematic every-`P`-th-row sample cycles through all
packets. A single period-`P` stripe *cannot* also guarantee every arbitrary
strided sample in its first `P` terms --- that is mathematically incompatible
with the contiguous guarantee --- so heavy arbitrary strides rely on the
redundancy `r`, not on the stripe.

## What the format cannot do

Three limits are worth stating plainly:

* **Deleting every `_schema` column** removes the in-band schema entirely. Use
  the sidecar (`cs_write(..., sidecar = TRUE)`), which is independent, or accept
  that the file reads back as character columns with `status = "absent"`.
* **Case-folding every cell** is detected, not recovered: the per-packet CRC
  covers the exact-case payload, so folded payloads fail and are dropped.
* **`NA` versus `""`**: with the default `missingValues = [""]`, an empty cell
  reads back as `NA`; the two are indistinguishable once written with
  `na = ""`. Numeric values are written at R's default precision.

Erasure coding (which would recover from fewer surviving rows but destroy human
readability and add a dependency) is reserved for a future version; the `E`
packet type is left unused for it.
